bihar_raw_news.title: Bihar Tightens Midday Meal Checks After Food-Quality Complaints
bihar_raw_news.content: Home Breaking News Bihar Tightens Midday Meal Checks After Food-Quality Complaints Breaking News Bihar Tightens Midday Meal Checks After Food-Quality Complaints By Maria Dsouza November 7, 2026 0 Copy URL Facebook Linkedin X WhatsApp Bihar has ordered headmasters of government and government-aided schools to taste and certify midday meals before they are served to students, following complaints about poor food quality. The directive requires a daily record confirming that the meal was tasted, found satisfactory and considered fit for consumption. The order was communicated through an IPRD communique on Friday, which said the directorate of the Mid-Day Meal Scheme had instructed all district education officers to enforce the procedure in schools. The directive places responsibility for the immediate pre-serving check on the school’s headmaster, teacher-in-charge or principal teacher. Under the new procedure, the designated school official must taste the meal every day before it is distributed to students. The official must then certify that the food was tasted, was satisfactory and was fit for consumption. The requirement applies to schools covered by the state’s government and government-aided education system. If the headmaster, teacher-in-charge or principal teacher is absent, a nominated teacher must carry out the tasting and certification. This provision ensures that the daily check does not stop because the school’s senior officials are unavailable, according to the reported directive. The certificate must be signed by the headmaster or teacher-in-charge and retained in the school’s records. These records are intended to be available for official verification, creating a documentary trail for district education authorities to check whether the procedure has been followed. The directive comes after reports of poor-quality food in schools, making the school-level certification process the latest administrative response to concerns over the midday meal system. While the order assigns a clear responsibility to school officials, the report does not specify any new testing arrangement, inspection schedule, penalty for non-compliance or changes to the agencies supplying the meals. The role of district education officers will be to enforce the instruction across the state’s government and aided schools. For students, the immediate change is that a designated school representative must taste the meal before serving and maintain a signed certificate in the school records. Further implementation details will depend on how the education authorities verify these certificates and respond to any future complaints about meal quality. bihar_raw_news.title: Bihar Expands Solar Power Plan for Rural Water Towers - Urban Acres
bihar_raw_news.content: Home Breaking News Bihar Expands Solar Power Plan for Rural Water Towers Breaking News Bihar Expands Solar Power Plan for Rural Water Towers By Maria Dsouza November 7, 2026 0 Copy URL Facebook Linkedin X WhatsApp Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary has directed officials to raise the proposed capacity of solar panels on rural water towers from 5 kilowatts to 20 kilowatts, linking the expansion to improved panchayat services, energy savings and more reliable basic infrastructure. Choudhary issued the instructions while chairing a review meeting of the panchayati raj department at the Sankalp auditorium in Lok Sevak Awas. He asked officials to install the higher-capacity panels in a way that allows panchayats to derive greater benefits from the solarisation of rural water infrastructure. The original proposal presented at the meeting involved installing 5-kilowatt off-grid solar panels on water towers under the Chief Minister Gramin Peyjal Nishchay Yojana. Panchayati raj department secretary Manoj Kumar briefed the chief minister on the proposed scheme, its implementation procedures, annual electricity expenditure and the department’s responsibilities. The revised 20-kilowatt capacity is intended to support basic facilities in panchayats while reducing energy consumption and expenditure. The meeting also discussed how savings generated through solarisation could be used, although the department’s presentation did not specify the amount of savings expected or the facilities that would receive the funds. Choudhary asked officials to make the solarisation of Panchayat Sarkar buildings an integral part of construction estimates. He also directed the department to link the work to funds from the 15th Finance Commission and the 7th State Finance Commission to ensure timely availability of funds and faster implementation. The plan will involve the Bihar Renewable Energy Development Agency, or BREDA. The department said BREDA’s role would cover implementation, financial management, maintenance and monitoring of the solar panels. An implementation and coordination committee is also proposed to oversee the programme. The review meeting additionally focused on monitoring electricity supply in panchayats. Choudhary ordered officials to regularly share information on the number of hours of power supply received by each panchayat with public representatives. A dedicated team is to be set up to send daily updates to the designated mobile numbers of panchayat mukhiyas, MLAs and MPs. The electricity-monitoring mechanism would create a regular flow of information on local power availability, but the department’s presentation did not state when the updates would begin or identify the system that would be used to collect and verify the data. Choudhary also directed officials to accelerate construction of Panchayat Sarkar buildings and ensure their maintenance and regular upkeep. He said contractors responsible for constructing the buildings should also be held accountable for maintenance through a mechanism that clearly defines their responsibilities and liability. The next steps are the preparation of implementation arrangements for the higher-capacity solar panels, coordination with BREDA and the identification of financing through the two Finance Commission funds. Officials are also expected to establish the team responsible for daily electricity-supply updates and clarify maintenance responsibilities for Panchayat Sarkar buildings. Share Copy

On 3 November 2026, Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary announced that Bihar has become the first state in India to introduce a comprehensive Silt Management Policy to address recurring floods and promote the scientific utilisation of river silt. Key Points Silt Management Policy: Bihar has introduced the Bihar Water Sources Restoration and Silt Management Policy, 2026. It aims to restore rivers and water bodies through scientific desilting. It seeks to improve river water-carrying capacity and reduce flood risks. Nadi Sanjeevani Initiative: An MoU was signed between the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) and the Government of Bihar on 3 November 2026. It aims to utilise excavated silt in National Highway construction projects. Utilisation of Silt: 243 lakh cubic metres of silt will be utilised in 16 ongoing National Highway projects. Another 835 lakh cubic metres is proposed for 27 future projects, subject to technical suitability. Implementation: The Bihar Road Construction Department (RCD) will act as the nodal department. A State-level Coordination Committee will oversee implementation. Benefits of the Policy: Reduction in flood risks through scientific desilting. Restoration of rivers and water bodies. Protection of agricultural land affected by sand and silt deposition. Sustainable utilisation of silt in infrastructure development. Assistance to Farmers: Financial assistance of ₹20,000 per two hectares is provided to affected farmers for excavating deposited sand. bihar_raw_news.title: NHAI to Use Bihar River Silt for Highway Construction - RAHSTA Expo
bihar_raw_news.content: NHAI to Use Bihar River Silt for Highway Construction Infrastructure Transport Nov 06 2026 The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) and the Bihar government have signed a Memorandum of Understanding for scientifically desilting water bodies and using suitable excavated silt in national highway projects. The initiative, named Nadi Sanjivani, Nadi Punarjeevan, Sadak Navnirman, is intended to address silt accumulation, seasonal flooding and the shortage of construction materials in the state. Rivers including the Ganga, Kosi, Gandak, Falgu and Bagmati carry substantial silt through Bihar. The accumulation reduces their water-carrying capacity and complicates water management, while the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has faced delays and higher costs because soil and ballast often have to be transported from distant locations. Under the agreement, 39.3 mn cubic metres of silt will be made available at no cost for ongoing highway projects. A further 105 mn cubic metres is planned for future projects. The NHAI will lead dredging using scientific methods, with the material being used for earthwork, embankments and subgrade construction. The NHAI is executing 39 projects covering 1,561 km in Bihar, with an investment of Rs. 583.4 bn. It has also proposed 11 projects covering 1,982 km at an estimated cost of Rs. 1.85 tn. The programme will cover waterways linked to projects including Manikpur-Sahebganj, Munger-Mirzachauki, the Bhagalpur Bypass-Rasulpur route and the Varanasi-Ranchi-Kolkata corridor. The plan draws on Maharashtra’s Buldhana Pattern, under which excavated soil was used in highway construction while ponds and water bodies were widened and deepened. That initiative used 22.5 mn cubic metres of soil and increased water storage capacity by 22.5 mn cubic metres without cost to the state government. Bihar has also planned 1,800 km of expressways under Vision 2047, and successful desilting could support their construction. Tags: NHAI Bihar river desilting

national_raw_news.title: India beat Japan 4-1 to retain Men’s Asian Champions Trophy 11 hours ago 340
national_raw_news.content: In hockey, it was ‘Chak Dey’ moment for the defending champion India as the team lifted the trophy for the 6th time by defeating Japan 4-1 in the finals of 9th Hero Asian Hockey Championship at the Olympian Balbir Singh Senior International Hockey Stadium in Mohali, last evening. Akashvani Correspondent reports that the jubilant crowd and the Nation celebrated the win as a Diwali gift by the hockey boys ahead of the festival. Although this was India’s third successive title, the winning team had to earn it against a strong defence by the rival team. An early lead by the Samurais kept the Indian Tigers on the toes till the end of the 3rd quarter, when they equalised the goal. The fourth and last quarter was dominated by India as the boys striked thrice to take an unassailable lead and won the Gold. India’s title-winning run was a perfect farewell to midfielder Nilakanta Sharma, who played his last international match in the national jersey. In another match for Bronze, Malaysia defeated South Korea by 5-2 . Celebrating India’s title win, Hockey India has announced a cash reward of Rs. 3 lakhs for each player and 1.5 lakhs for each member of the support staff.

national_raw_news.title: Govt building modern sports ecosystem through Khelo India and TOPS, says PM Modi 9 hours ago 448
national_raw_news.content: Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that the government is building a modern sports ecosystem through school and grassroots programmes, Khelo India Centres and Olympic-standard training under the Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS). Felicitating India’s Asian Para Games 2026 contingent for its record haul of 114 medals, Prime Minister urged the athletes to build on their success as they prepare for the Los Angeles 2028 Games. Prime Minister also recalled his appeal from the Red Fort encouraging young people to participate in a nationwide talent hunt with the Olympics in focus. He said Para-sports also receive equal priority under these initiatives. Interacting with the contingent at the Indira Gandhi Sports Complex in New Delhi, PM Modi said the performance reflected India’s emergence as a major global sporting power. He congratulated the athletes, their families, coaches and trainers, saying the players had won both medals and the hearts of millions. India secured 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, alongside five world records and nine Asian records. Comparing the achievement with the country’s tally of 14 medals, including one gold, in 2010, PM Modi credited the athletes’ perseverance and dedication. The Prime Minister noted that 34 of the contingent’s 56 female athletes won medals, while Indian competitors swept all three podium positions in four events. The team also won nine gold medals on the final day. Highlighting individual performances, PM Modi said Mona Agarwal set a world record in para shooting, while Haney improved his own world record. He also praised Himanshu, Ravi and Jehan for overcoming physical challenges through their performances. Recalling the sacrifices behind sporting success, PM Modi spoke about Rinku, who lost his mother two months before the Games and held up her photograph after winning gold. “That moment made all of us emotional,” he said. The Prime Minister also highlighted the achievements of younger athletes, noting that 36 of the 61 debutants won medals and Sandeep set a world record on his debut. Describing sports as a means of personality development and nation-building, PM Modi said it teaches discipline, teamwork and the ability to recover from setbacks. He added that the expansion of sports infrastructure, equipment manufacturing and broadcasting was creating employment opportunities beyond the playing field.

national_raw_news.content: Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi said India expects to exceed its 220 billion dollar investment target for adding 190 GW of non-fossil fuel power capacity by 2030. Addressing the media at the conclusion of the Bharat Renewable Energy (BRE) Summit 2026, the Union Minister said that investments totalling 7 lakh crore rupees, including domestic funds and foreign direct investment, have flowed into the renewable energy sector over the past two years. Mr Joshi said the momentum would continue and India would meet the 500 GW target on schedule. He added that strategies are also being prepared to add another 300 GW as directed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He said that at present, the country’s installed power capacity from non-fossil fuels stands at 310 GW, and the Union government has fixed a target of reaching 500 GW by 2030. Meanwhile, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy Secretary, Santosh Kumar Sarangi said the government is preparing new guidelines for recycling solar module waste. The Summit was inaugurated by Prime Minister on 2nd November 2026. In his address, the Prime Minister highlighted the strategic importance of India’s sustained investments in renewable energy in strengthening the country’s resilience to global disruptions, arising from COVID-19 pandemic and the West Asia crisis. He observed that India’s investment in the renewable energy sector has largely shielded the country from these disruptions.

national_raw_news.title: From snow leopards to coral reefs: India’s biosphere reserves connect conservation with livelihoods
national_raw_news.content: In the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve, an invasive shrub is finding a second life as elephant sculptures, furniture and handicrafts. Indigenous artisans use uprooted Lantana vines to create objects that support livelihoods while drawing attention to the damage the plant causes to forests. In 2021, 125 life-sized Lantana elephants were displayed in London, carrying a message of coexistence with wildlife. Similar sculptures have appeared at Bengaluru Airport, across Bengaluru and at Rashtrapati Bhavan. The initiative illustrates the idea at the heart of biosphere reserves: protecting nature while creating opportunities for the people who depend on it. As the International Day for Biosphere Reserves is observed on November 3, India’s network of 18 notified reserves demonstrates how conservation, scientific research and sustainable livelihoods can work together. Thirteen of these reserves belong to UNESCO’s World Network of Biosphere Reserves, the highest number in South Asia. The landscapes range from the forests of the Western Ghats and the mangroves of the Sundarbans to the coral reefs of the Gulf of Mannar and the high-altitude Cold Desert of Himachal Pradesh. Conservation beyond protected boundaries India is one of the world’s 17 mega-biodiverse countries. Despite occupying only 2.4 per cent of Earth’s land area, it accounts for approximately 7–8 per cent of recorded species worldwide. Protecting this diversity requires attention to habitats, species and genetic variation, alongside the needs of communities that rely on natural resources. Biosphere reserves provide a framework for bringing these objectives together. While national parks and wildlife sanctuaries primarily protect wildlife and habitats under India’s wildlife protection laws, biosphere reserves take a broader approach, connecting protected ecosystems with surrounding settlements and economic activities. UNESCO’s Man and the Biosphere Programme, launched in 1971, promotes scientific approaches to improving relationships between people and their environment. Biosphere reserves serve as living laboratories where sustainable development practices can be tested and demonstrated. Their work combines three functions: conserving biodiversity and landscapes, supporting environmentally responsible economic development, and advancing research, monitoring, education and training. Three zones, connected purposes A biosphere reserve’s structure reflects this balance. Its core area provides the highest level of protection, conserving habitats, species and genetic resources. Human activity is strictly limited, with compatible research and monitoring supporting conservation. The surrounding or adjoining buffer zone accommodates activities such as environmental education, scientific research and regulated ecotourism. These help build ecological understanding while reducing pressure on the core. The transition area supports settlements and livelihoods, including responsible agriculture, sustainable forestry and locally appropriate tourism. Globally, core areas account for an average of 18 per cent of biosphere reserves, buffer zones for 30 per cent and transition areas for 52 per cent. The distribution underlines the importance of inhabited, working landscapes within the conservation model. A network spanning India’s ecological diversity Nilgiri, designated in 1986, was India’s first biosphere reserve. It entered UNESCO’s World Network in 2000. Spread across 5,520 square kilometres in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka, the reserve includes tropical evergreen forests, montane shola forests and grasslands. Its wildlife includes the endangered lion-tailed macaque and Nilgiri tahr, as well as elephants, tigers, gaur, sambar and chital. The landscape supports more than 100 mammal species and 550 bird species. At a different ecological extreme, Himachal Pradesh’s Cold Desert Biosphere Reserve covers 7,770 square kilometres at elevations between 3,300 and 6,600 metres. Included in UNESCO’s network in 2025, it supports snow leopards, Himalayan ibex and blue sheep, alongside 732 vascular plant species, including 30 endemics. Around 12,000 people live in this demanding environment. Their livelihoods draw on pastoralism, yak and goat herding, barley and pea cultivation, and Tibetan herbal medicine. Off Tamil Nadu’s southeastern coast, the Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve brings together coral reefs, seagrass beds and mangroves across approximately 10,500 square kilometres. These linked ecosystems support 4,223 plant and animal species. The reserve sustains around 25 lakh people across a region that includes approximately 47 coastal villages. The other Indian reserves recognised by UNESCO are Nanda Devi, Nokrek, Sundarbans, Great Nicobar, Similipal, Pachmarhi, Khangchendzonga, Agasthyamalai, Achanakmar-Amarkantak and Panna. Manas, Dibru-Saikhowa, Dehang-Dibang, Great Rann of Kutch and Seshachalam complete India’s nationally notified network. national_raw_news.title: More than 21,000 devotees pay homage to sacred relics of Shakyamuni Buddha at Tawang ...
national_raw_news.content: More than 21,000 devotees pay homage to sacred relics of Shakyamuni Buddha at Tawang Monastery Toggle navigation हिंदी खबर More than 21,000 devotees pay homage to sacred relics of Shakyamuni Buddha at Tawang Monastery ANI | Updated: Nov 06, 2026 11:38 IST ANI News Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], November 6 (ANI): More than 21,000 devotees have visited Gaden Namgyal Lhatse (Tawang Monastery) so far to offer prayers and pay homage to the sacred relics of Shakyamuni Buddha. According to a press release issued by the Ministry of Culture, devotees from Tawang and neighbouring regions of Arunachal Pradesh have been gathering at the monastery to seek blessings in the presence of the sacred relics. The exposition at Tawang Monastery will remain open to the public until November 7. The exposition holds special historical and spiritual significance as the sacred relics have returned to Arunachal Pradesh after a gap of 13 years, the release said. Brought from the National Museum, New Delhi, the relics offer Buddhist monks, nuns, devotees and the general public an opportunity to pay homage to the sacred remains of Shakyamuni Buddha and deepen their engagement with India's rich Buddhist heritage. The sacred relics were discovered at Piprahwah in Uttar Pradesh in 1898. Their discovery marked an important milestone in the archaeological history of Buddhism . Preserved at the National Museum, New Delhi, the relics hold immense historical, archaeological and spiritual significance for Buddhist communities, the release noted. Two special exhibitions have also been organised at Tawang Monastery to highlight the rich legacy of Buddhism . ‘Unearthing the Sacred Piprahwa: The Story of the Holy Buddha Relics and Their Discovery’ by the International Buddhist Confederation (IBC) traces the discovery and historical significance of the relics. ‘Crossroads of Dhamma: Classical Legacies, Living Art, and Anthropological Perspectives’, curated by the National Museum, New Delhi, showcases the historical, artistic and cultural dimensions of Buddhism . Following the exposition at Tawang Monastery, the sacred relics will be taken to TGL Monastery (Lower Gompa), Bomdilla, from November 8 to 13, 2026, and thereafter to the Golden Pagoda, Namsai, from November 14 to 20, 2026. The Holi relics are scheduled to return to the National Museum, New Delhi, on November 21, the release said. The exposition is being organised by the Ministry of Culture, Government of India in collaboration with the International Buddhist Confederation and the Government of Arunachal Pradesh. The initiative reflects the Government of India's commitment to preserving and promoting the country's rich Buddhist heritage and disseminating the timeless teachings of Bhagwan Buddha, centred on peace, compassion, wisdom and universal brotherhood. national_raw_news.title: India Successfully Tests Quasi-Ballistic Missile 'Pralay' Off Odisha Coast, Paving Way For ...
national_raw_news.content: India Successfully Tests Quasi-Ballistic Missile 'Pralay' Off Odisha Coast, Paving Way For Induction Into Armed Forces Defence India Successfully Tests Quasi-Ballistic Missile 'Pralay' Off Odisha Coast, Paving Way For Induction Into Armed Forces Swarajya Staff Nov 06, 2026 | Updated 08:20 AM GMT+5:30 Save & read from anywhere! Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app . Sign In Prefer Prefer Pralay Missile test (Pic Via PIB) India successfully flight-tested its indigenously developed Pralay quasi-ballistic missile off the Odisha coast on Thursday (5 November), marking a significant advancement towards operational induction into the armed forces. The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) conducted the test from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island as part of user evaluation trials. The missile met all stipulated objectives , with performance data captured and validated by various range instruments deployed by the Integrated Test Range at Chandipur. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh described the trial as another significant milestone in strengthening India's indigenous defence capabilities. Research Centre Imarat in Hyderabad developed the missile in collaboration with other DRDO laboratories, whilst Bharat Dynamics Limited produced the system as one of the Development-cum-Production Partners. The successful test was conducted in the presence of senior DRDO officials, armed forces representatives and industry partners. Pralay is a solid-propellant surface-to-surface missile with a range of 150 to 500 kilometres and a payload capacity of 500 to 1,000 kilogrammes. The system employs state-of-the-art guidance and navigation technology, including an advanced Inertial Navigation System and Radio Frequency seeker to ensure high precision. The quasi-ballistic design enables the missile to follow a lower altitude trajectory with in-flight manoeuvres, making it significantly harder to intercept compared to traditional ballistic missiles. Defence Secretary and DRDO Chairman Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed that the successful test brings the system's induction into the armed forces imminent, enhancing India's operational preparedness against emerging threats.
